title: EFFECTS OF COLOUR OF LIGHT ON NONVISUAL PSYCHOLOGICAL PROCESSES
research_question: This study investigated the influence of colour of light ('warm, 'cool' and artificial 'daylight' white lighting) on subjects' self-reported mood, cognitive performance and room light estimation.

participants.description: 108 high school students (54 females, 54 males), aged 18 years, from the same high school with similar education background.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A neutrally designed and coloured windowless chamber (3.9 × 3.8 × 2.5m) with off-white walls/ceiling and off-white/grey floor. Lighting provided by six recessed fluorescent lamp luminaries with prismatic lens refractors. Illuminance was held constant at 500 lux. Air temperature 21°C, ambient noise 36-38 dBA. Three types of 36W T8 lamps were used: 'Warm' white (3000 K, reddish, CRI 95), 'Cool' white (4000 K, bluish, CRI 95), and Artificial 'daylight' white (5500 K, even more bluish, CRI 95).

measures.instrument: Multiple choice questions about a text (18 questions)
General recall questions about a text (6 questions)

mechanisms: Cognitive processes of short-term memory and attention operating in tasks were impaired by more bluish light ('cool' and artificial 'daylight') compared to 'warm' white lighting.
Selective operations and capacity limits of attention in problem solving were enhanced by 'warm' compared to 'cool' and artificial 'daylight' white lighting.
Gender differences in emotional reaction to colour of light may be attributable to the socialization of gender differences in emotional experience and functioning (Knez & Kers, 2000).
implementation_implications: The findings suggest that 'warm' white lighting may be beneficial for short-term recall and problem-solving tasks.
limitations: The PANAS instrument may not adequately conceptualize self-reported affect data, raising questions about its suitability for this research.
The study did not obtain a direct mood effect, leaving the mediation of cognitive effects by affect as an open question.
The study did not include a cognitive task measuring attentional accuracy and/or speed, which could clarify underlying mechanisms.
